sets.title: Hard
sets.about: Counting and classifying, where a yes or no would be a guess. You need the complete invariant, not a hint of one.

sets.title: Moves
sets.about: The habits editorials assume: what the constraints are telling you, and which first move to make. Judgement calls, not computed answers.

sets.title: Invariants
sets.about: Can it be done, or what must the answer be? Look for the quantity no move can change.

sets.title: Games
sets.about: Two players, perfect play. Label small positions as won or lost and look for the pattern.

sets.title: Bits
sets.about: XOR, AND and OR, one binary digit at a time.

sets.title: Binary strings
sets.about: Blocks, boundaries, inversions and balances: the handful of views that settle most binary-string problems.

sets.title: Palindromes
sets.about: Centres, mirrors, parities of letter counts, and the facts about periods that setters assume.

puzzles.prompt: The numbers 1 to 10 are on a board. You repeatedly erase two numbers and write their sum. What number is left at the end?
puzzles.verify: result = sum(range(1, 11))
puzzles.showed: The total on the board never changes: it is always 55.

puzzles.prompt: The numbers 1 to 6 are on a board. You repeatedly erase two numbers and write their difference (larger minus smaller). Can the last number be 0?
puzzles.showed: Replacing a and b by a - b changes the total by 2b, an even amount. The total starts at 21, odd, so it can never be 0.

puzzles.prompt: Same game with the numbers 1 to 7. Can the last number be 0?
puzzles.showed: Now the total is 28, even, so parity does not forbid it, and it can be done: for example 7-6, 5-4, 3-2 leave 1, 1, 1, 1, then 1-1 twice, then 0-0.

puzzles.prompt: An island has 13 red, 15 green and 17 blue chameleons. When two of different colours meet, both change to the third colour. Can all the chameleons ever be the same colour?
puzzles.showed: A meeting changes each colour count by -1, -1, +2, so the difference between any two counts changes by 0 or 3. The differences start as 2, 2 and 4, never multiples of 3, but all one colour needs two counts equal to 0.

puzzles.prompt: Same island, but with 1 red, 4 green and 7 blue chameleons. Can they all become the same colour?
puzzles.showed: Here all the differences are multiples of 3, so the invariant allows it, and it can be done: red meets blue once (0, 6, 6), then green meets blue six times.

puzzles.prompt: Five coins show heads. A move turns over exactly two coins. Can you make all five show tails?
puzzles.showed: Turning two coins changes the number of heads by -2, 0 or +2. It starts odd and stays odd.

puzzles.prompt: Six coins show heads. A move turns over exactly three coins. What is the smallest number of moves that makes all six show tails?
puzzles.showed: Each move changes the parity of the number of heads, so an even number of moves is needed; two are enough (three coins, then the other three).

puzzles.prompt: Seven cups stand upright. A move turns over exactly four cups. Can all seven end up upside down?
puzzles.showed: Turning four cups changes the number of upright cups by an even amount. Seven is odd; zero is even.

puzzles.prompt: A board shows the number 1. A move either multiplies it by 3 or adds 6. Can the board ever show 100?
puzzles.showed: Look at the remainder mod 6. Adding 6 keeps it; multiplying by 3 turns 1 into 3 and keeps 3 as 3. So the board only ever shows numbers that are 1 or 3 mod 6, and 100 is 4 mod 6.

puzzles.prompt: You have the pair (1, 1). A move replaces (a, b) by (a + b, b) or by (a, a + b). Can you reach (6, 9)?
puzzles.showed: Adding one number to the other never changes their greatest common divisor. It starts at 1, and gcd(6, 9) = 3.

puzzles.prompt: Same moves from (1, 1). Can you reach (5, 8)?
puzzles.showed: gcd(5, 8) = 1, so nothing forbids it; run the subtraction backwards: (5,8), (5,3), (2,3), (2,1), (1,1).

puzzles.prompt: A 3 by 3 grid holds zeros. A move adds 1 to every cell of one row or of one column. Can you reach the grid that has a 1 in the top-left corner and zeros everywhere else?
puzzles.verify:
import itertools
ok = False
for r in itertools.product(range(3), repeat=3):
    for c in itertools.product(range(3), repeat=3):
        g = [[r[i] + c[j] for j in range(3)] for i in range(3)]
        if g == [[1, 0, 0], [0, 0, 0], [0, 0, 0]]: ok = True
result = 0 if ok else 1
puzzles.showed: Take any 2 by 2 block of cells: (top-left + bottom-right) minus (top-right + bottom-left) never changes, because a row or column adds to one cell of each pair. It starts at 0, and the target has 1 there.

puzzles.prompt: Six numbers sit round a circle: 1, 0, 0, 0, 0, 0. A move adds 1 to two neighbouring numbers. Can all six become equal?
puzzles.showed: Colour the positions alternately black and white. Every move adds 1 to one black and one white position, so (black total minus white total) stays 1 for ever; all equal would make it 0.

puzzles.prompt: Now five numbers round a circle: 1, 0, 0, 0, 0, with the same move. Can all five become equal?
puzzles.showed: With an odd circle the alternate colouring is impossible, and the obstacle disappears: add to positions 2-3 and to positions 4-5 and everything is 1. An invariant must be checked, not assumed.

puzzles.prompt: A row reads 1 2 3 4. A move swaps two neighbouring numbers. Can the row read 2 1 4 3 after exactly three moves?
puzzles.showed: Every swap of neighbours changes the number of out-of-order pairs by exactly 1. The target has two such pairs, so the number of moves must be even.

puzzles.prompt: A row reads 1 2 3 4 5. A move takes three neighbouring numbers a b c and turns them into b c a. Can the row ever read 2 1 3 4 5?
puzzles.showed: Turning a b c into b c a is two swaps of neighbours, so the number of out-of-order pairs changes by an even amount. The target has exactly one such pair.

puzzles.prompt: A knight stands on a corner square of a chessboard. Can it be on the opposite corner after exactly seven moves?
puzzles.showed: Each knight move changes the colour of its square. Opposite corners have the same colour, so the number of moves must be even.

puzzles.prompt: What is the smallest number of moves a knight needs to get from one corner of a chessboard to the opposite corner?
puzzles.showed: The colour argument says it must be even; the distance (14 steps of row plus column, at most 3 per move) says at least 5; so at least 6, and 6 is possible.

puzzles.prompt: Five people are at a party. Can it happen that each of them shakes hands with exactly three of the others?
puzzles.showed: Add up the handshakes per person: each handshake is counted twice, so the total must be even. Five times three is 15.

puzzles.prompt: And with six people, each shaking hands with exactly three of the others?
puzzles.showed: Six times three is 18, even, so the count allows it; two groups of three, everyone shaking hands with the whole other group, does it.

puzzles.prompt: Four lamps in a row are off. A move switches two neighbouring lamps (on becomes off, off becomes on). Can you reach a state with exactly one lamp on?
puzzles.showed: A move changes the number of lit lamps by -2, 0 or +2, so it stays even.

puzzles.prompt: Same four lamps, all off. What is the smallest number of moves after which only the first and the last lamp are on?
puzzles.showed: Switch lamps 1-2, then 2-3, then 3-4: the inner lamps are each switched twice.

puzzles.prompt: Three frogs sit at the points 0, 1 and 2 of a number line. A move lets one frog leap over another, landing the same distance beyond it. Can the frogs ever occupy the points 0, 1 and 3?
puzzles.showed: A frog at x leaping over y lands at 2y - x, which has the same parity as x. So there are always two frogs on even points and one on an odd point; 0, 1, 3 has it the other way round.

puzzles.prompt: A token is at 0 on a number line. A move shifts it by 3 or by 5, in either direction. What is the smallest number of moves that puts it at 1?
puzzles.showed: 3 + 3 - 5 = 1. Every point is reachable because gcd(3, 5) = 1; each move changes the parity, so an odd number of moves is needed and one move is not enough.

puzzles.prompt: Now a move shifts the token by 4 or by 6, in either direction, starting from 0. Can it reach 9?
puzzles.showed: Every move keeps the position even.

puzzles.prompt: Write a plus or a minus sign in front of each of the numbers 1, 2, ..., 10 and add everything up. Can the result be 0?
puzzles.showed: Changing a plus to a minus changes the total by an even amount. With all pluses the total is 55, odd.

puzzles.prompt: And with the numbers 1, 2, ..., 11?
puzzles.showed: The total 66 is even, so each side must reach 33; for example 11 + 10 + 9 + 3 = 33.

puzzles.prompt: A 4 by 4 board has two opposite corner squares removed. Can the remaining 14 squares be covered by 7 dominoes?
puzzles.showed: Colour it like a chessboard. Opposite corners have the same colour, so 8 squares of one colour and 6 of the other remain, and each domino covers one of each.

puzzles.prompt: Now remove instead the two corner squares at the ends of the same side. Can the remaining 14 squares be covered by 7 dominoes?
puzzles.showed: These two corners have different colours, so 7 of each colour remain, and a covering exists (lay the shortened row flat and the rest in rows).

puzzles.prompt: A row of digits reads 1100. A move finds a 1 immediately followed by a 0 and swaps them. How many moves are made before no move is possible?
puzzles.verify:
s, n = list('1100'), 0
while True:
    i = next((i for i in range(3) if s[i] == '1' and s[i + 1] == '0'), None)
    if i is None: break
    s[i], s[i + 1] = s[i + 1], s[i]; n += 1
result = n
puzzles.showed: Count the pairs (a 1, a later 0): there are 4, and each move removes exactly one. The count can only go down, so the process must stop.

puzzles.prompt: A knockout tournament has 25 players. Each match eliminates exactly one player (some players may get a free pass in a round). How many matches are played until one champion remains?
puzzles.verify: result = 25 - 1
puzzles.showed: Every match removes exactly one player, and 24 players must be removed, however the rounds are arranged.

puzzles.prompt: A pile has 21 stones. Two players take turns removing 1, 2 or 3 stones; whoever takes the last stone wins. How many stones should the first player take to be sure of winning?
puzzles.showed: Leave a multiple of 4. Whatever the opponent takes, answer so that the two of you remove 4 between you.

puzzles.prompt: Same game with 20 stones. Who wins with perfect play?
puzzles.showed: 20 is a multiple of 4: whatever the first player takes, the second completes it to 4.

puzzles.prompt: A pile has 7 stones. Players take turns removing 1 or 2 stones, and now whoever takes the last stone LOSES. Who wins with perfect play?
puzzles.showed: Being left with 1 stone loses. From 4 you must leave 3 or 2, from which the opponent leaves you 1; so 1, 4, 7 are the losing piles for the player to move.

puzzles.prompt: Two piles of 5 stones each. A move removes any positive number of stones from one pile; whoever takes the last stone wins. Who wins?
puzzles.showed: The second player copies: whatever is taken from one pile, take the same from the other. The piles stay equal, so the second player always has a move.

puzzles.prompt: Same game with piles of 5 and 7. Who wins?
puzzles.showed: The first player takes 2 from the larger pile, making them equal, and then copies.

puzzles.prompt: Three piles of 1, 2 and 3 stones, same rules (any number from one pile, last stone wins). Who wins?
puzzles.showed: Whatever the first player does, the second can leave two equal piles, or one pile cleared and two equal. In binary: 1 xor 2 xor 3 = 0, and a position with XOR 0 is lost for the player to move.

puzzles.prompt: Three piles of 3, 4 and 5 stones, same rules. Who wins?
puzzles.showed: 3 xor 4 xor 5 = 2, not 0, so the first player can move to a position with XOR 0.

puzzles.prompt: In that game (piles 3, 4, 5) the first player has exactly one winning move, and it is in the pile of 3. How many stones are left in that pile afterwards?
puzzles.showed: The XOR of all piles is 2. Change the pile of 3 to 3 xor 2 = 1; now 1 xor 4 xor 5 = 0.

puzzles.prompt: A chocolate bar of 3 by 5 squares. A move breaks one piece into two along a line; whoever makes the last possible break wins. Who wins?
puzzles.verify:
breaks = 3 * 5 - 1
result = 0 if breaks % 2 == 1 else 1
puzzles.showed: Every break adds one piece, so there are always exactly 14 breaks. Fourteen is even: the second player makes the last one, whatever anyone does.

puzzles.prompt: The number 10 is on a board. A move subtracts from it one of its divisors other than itself. The player who cannot move (because the number is 1) loses. Who wins?
puzzles.showed: An odd number has only odd divisors, so it always becomes even. From an even number subtract 1 to hand over an odd number. The player holding even numbers never gets stuck at 1.

puzzles.prompt: Same game starting from 9. Who wins?
puzzles.showed: From an odd number every move produces an even number, and the opponent then subtracts 1.

puzzles.prompt: What is 13 XOR 7? (XOR compares the binary digits: 1 where they differ, 0 where they agree.)
puzzles.verify: result = 13 ^ 7
puzzles.showed: 1101 and 0111 differ in the 8s place and the 2s place: 1010.

puzzles.prompt: What is 1 XOR 2 XOR 3 XOR ... XOR 100?
puzzles.verify:
import functools, operator
result = functools.reduce(operator.xor, range(1, 101))
puzzles.showed: Each block 4k, 4k+1, 4k+2, 4k+3 XORs to 0, so 0 to 99 cancel completely and only 100 remains.

puzzles.prompt: In the list 5, 3, 5, 7, 3 every number but one appears an even number of times. XOR all five together. What do you get?
puzzles.showed: Equal numbers cancel in pairs, in any order, leaving the one without a partner.

puzzles.prompt: Two numbers have XOR equal to 6 and AND equal to 8. What is their sum?
puzzles.verify: result = next(a + b for a in range(64) for b in range(64) if a ^ b == 6 and a & b == 8)
puzzles.showed: XOR adds without carrying, AND marks where carries happen: sum = XOR + 2 x AND = 6 + 16.

puzzles.prompt: How many numbers x from 0 to 15 satisfy x AND 5 = x?
puzzles.verify: result = sum(1 for x in range(16) if x & 5 == x)
puzzles.showed: x may only use the bits that 5 has (the 4s and the 1s place), each either on or off: 0, 1, 4, 5.

puzzles.prompt: What is the largest value of a XOR b when a and b are both between 0 and 10?
puzzles.verify: result = max(a ^ b for a in range(11) for b in range(11))
puzzles.showed: 8 XOR 7 = 15: one number supplies the top bit, the other all the bits below it.

puzzles.prompt: What is the largest power of two that divides 40?
puzzles.verify: result = 40 & -40
puzzles.showed: 40 is 101000 in binary; the lowest 1 is in the 8s place.

puzzles.prompt: Two numbers, 5 and 3, are replaced by their AND and their OR. What is the sum of the two new numbers?
puzzles.showed: In each bit position, AND and OR together hold exactly as many 1s as the two originals did. So the sum never changes under this operation.

puzzles.prompt: For the list 1, 2, 3, add up a XOR b over the three pairs.
puzzles.showed: Bit by bit: in the 1s place two numbers have the bit and one does not, giving 2 x 1 differing pairs; the same in the 2s place. 2 x 1 + 2 x 2 = 6.

puzzles.prompt: How many subsets of {1, 2, 3, 4}, including the empty one, have XOR equal to 0?
puzzles.verify:
import itertools, functools, operator
result = sum(1 for k in range(5) for c in itertools.combinations((1, 2, 3, 4), k) if functools.reduce(operator.xor, c, 0) == 0)
puzzles.showed: Only the empty set and {1, 2, 3}. The numbers 1, 2, 4 are independent and 3 = 1 XOR 2, so there is exactly one relation.

puzzles.prompt: The numbers 1 to 7 are on a board. You repeatedly erase two numbers and write their XOR. What number is left at the end?
puzzles.verify:
import functools, operator
result = functools.reduce(operator.xor, range(1, 8))
puzzles.showed: The XOR of everything on the board never changes, and 1 XOR 2 XOR ... XOR 7 = 0.

puzzles.prompt: What is the smallest power of two that is at least 37?
puzzles.verify: result = 1 << (36).bit_length()
puzzles.showed: 32 is too small; the next is 64. A number y is a power of two exactly when y AND (y - 1) is 0.

puzzles.prompt: Nine bulbs in a 3 by 3 grid are off. A move switches every bulb in one row or in one column. Can you reach a state with exactly one bulb on?
puzzles.showed: Take any four bulbs forming the corners of a rectangle. A row or column move switches none or exactly two of them, so the number lit among those four stays even. One lit bulb would be alone in some such rectangle.

puzzles.prompt: Same grid, all off. What is the smallest number of moves that turns all nine bulbs on?
puzzles.showed: Each row once (or each column once). Fewer cannot work: every bulb must be switched an odd number of times, and one or two lines do not touch all nine.

puzzles.prompt: A row of signs reads + + - - -. A move replaces two neighbouring signs by one: a plus if they were equal, a minus if they were different. The last remaining sign is:
puzzles.showed: Think of + as 1 and - as -1: a move replaces two signs by their product. The product of everything never changes, and three minuses give -1.

puzzles.prompt: The numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 are written round a circle in that order. A move adds 1 to two neighbouring numbers. Can all six become equal?
puzzles.showed: Positions 1, 3, 5 hold 9 in total and positions 2, 4, 6 hold 12. Every move adds 1 to each group, so the gap of 3 never closes.

puzzles.prompt: Three glasses: two upright and one upside down. A move turns over exactly two glasses. Can all three end up upright?
puzzles.showed: Turning two glasses changes the number that are upside down by -2, 0 or +2. It starts at 1 and stays odd.

puzzles.prompt: A board shows the number 7. A move either multiplies it by 10 or adds 9. Can the board ever show 1000?
puzzles.showed: Both moves keep the remainder mod 9 (10 is 1 mod 9, and 9 is 0). The board always shows a number that is 7 mod 9, and 1000 is 1 mod 9.

puzzles.prompt: The numbers 1, 2, 3, 4 are on a board. You repeatedly erase two numbers a and b and write a + b + ab. What number is left at the end?
puzzles.showed: a + b + ab = (a + 1)(b + 1) - 1. So the product of (each number + 1) never changes: 2 x 3 x 4 x 5 = 120, and the last number is 119.

puzzles.prompt: The numbers 1 to 8 are on a board. You repeatedly erase two numbers a and b and write a + b - 1. What number is left at the end?
puzzles.showed: Each move lowers the total by exactly 1, and there are 7 moves: 36 - 7.

puzzles.prompt: A 4 by 4 board is all white. A move swaps the colours (white and black) of every cell in one row or one column. Can the board ever have exactly two black cells?
puzzles.showed: Among any four cells at the corners of a rectangle the number of black cells stays even. With exactly two black cells, some rectangle has just one of them at a corner.

puzzles.prompt: Five coins in a row show H T H T H. A move turns over two neighbouring coins. What is the smallest number of moves that makes all five show H?
puzzles.showed: Turn coins 2-3, then coins 3-4. The number of tails is even, so parity allows it; an odd number of tails would make it impossible.

puzzles.prompt: Five people are in a room; friendship is mutual. Can all five have different numbers of friends in the room?
puzzles.showed: The possible numbers are 0 to 4, so all five values would have to occur. But someone with 4 friends is friends with everyone, including the person with 0.

puzzles.prompt: You have a 6-litre jug and a 9-litre jug, a tap and a sink, and no markings. Can you end up with exactly 4 litres in one of the jugs?
puzzles.showed: Filling, emptying and pouring until one jug is full or the other empty always leaves amounts that are multiples of 3.

puzzles.prompt: With a 3-litre jug and a 5-litre jug instead, what is the smallest number of steps (a step is: fill a jug, empty a jug, or pour one into the other until one is full or empty) after which one jug holds exactly 4 litres?
puzzles.showed: Fill 5, pour into 3, empty 3, pour the remaining 2 into 3, fill 5, top up the 3: the 5 now holds 4. It is possible because gcd(3, 5) = 1.

puzzles.prompt: The row 5, 3, 8, 1 is sorted by repeatedly swapping two neighbours that are in the wrong order. How many swaps are made, whatever order you choose them in?
puzzles.verify:
a = [5, 3, 8, 1]
result = sum(1 for i in range(4) for j in range(i + 1, 4) if a[i] > a[j])
puzzles.showed: Each such swap removes exactly one out-of-order pair and creates none, and there are four of them: (5,3), (5,1), (3,1), (8,1).

puzzles.prompt: A dragon has 100 heads. A knight can cut off 15, 17, 20 or 5 heads with one blow (only if the dragon has at least that many), and then 24, 2, 14 or 17 heads grow back respectively. The dragon dies when it has no heads. Can the knight kill it?
puzzles.showed: The net changes are +9, -15, -6 and +12, all multiples of 3, and a killing blow must remove 15, 17, 20 or 5 exactly: the head count would have to be one of those, but it is always 1 more than a multiple of 3 and none of 15, 17, 20, 5 is.

puzzles.prompt: A 2 by 2 tray holds tiles 1, 2, 3 and one empty space: top row 1 2, bottom row 3 and the gap. A move slides a neighbouring tile into the gap. Can you reach: top row 2 1, bottom row 3 and the gap?
puzzles.showed: The tiles can only circulate round the tray, so their cyclic order (1, 2, 3 clockwise, skipping the gap) never changes. The target has them in the opposite cyclic order.

puzzles.prompt: An island has 7 red, 10 green and 17 blue chameleons. When two of different colours meet, both change to the third colour. Which single colour can all of them end up being?
puzzles.showed: Differences between counts change only by multiples of 3. For everyone to be blue, red and green must both reach 0, so red - green must be a multiple of 3: 7 - 10 = -3 works. The other two differences (10 and 7) do not.

puzzles.prompt: A bug sits on every square of a 5 by 5 board. At a signal every bug crawls to a square sharing a side with its own. Can every square again hold exactly one bug?
puzzles.showed: Colour the board like a chessboard: 13 squares of one colour and 12 of the other. Every bug changes colour, so 13 bugs would have to fit on 12 squares.

puzzles.prompt: The same on a 4 by 4 board: can every square again hold exactly one bug?
puzzles.showed: Now there are 8 squares of each colour, and it is easy: pair the squares up into dominoes and let the two bugs of each domino swap.

puzzles.prompt: On an unbounded chessboard, what is the smallest number of knight moves needed to reach the square immediately to the right of where the knight starts?
puzzles.showed: A knight changes square colour with every move and the neighbouring square has the other colour, so the number of moves is odd. One move is not enough; three are.

puzzles.prompt: A token starts at the point (0, 0) of a grid. A move changes both coordinates by 1 each, up or down independently. Can the token reach (3, 4)?
puzzles.showed: Each move changes x + y by -2, 0 or +2, so x + y stays even. 3 + 4 is odd.

puzzles.prompt: Take the number 7 to the 5th power, add up its digits, add up the digits of the result, and continue until a single digit is left. Which digit?
puzzles.showed: A number and the sum of its digits have the same remainder mod 9. 7^5 mod 9: 7, 4, 1, 7, 4. So the final digit is 4.

puzzles.prompt: Ten coins in a row show heads. A move turns over three coins in a row (neighbours). Can all ten be made to show tails?
puzzles.showed: Number the coins and group them by position mod 3: groups of 4, 3 and 3 coins. Each move flips exactly one coin of each group, so after m moves each group has flipped parity m times. The group of 4 needs m even, the groups of 3 need m odd.

puzzles.prompt: With nine coins in a row, all heads, and the same move (turn over three neighbours), what is the smallest number of moves that makes them all tails?
puzzles.showed: Coins 1-3, 4-6, 7-9. Here all three groups have 3 coins, so the parity conditions agree.

puzzles.prompt: A 3 by 3 board has the middle square of one side removed. Can the remaining 8 squares be covered by 4 dominoes?
puzzles.showed: Chessboard colouring: the 3 by 3 board has 5 squares of the corner colour and 4 of the other. The removed square is of the minority colour, leaving 5 and 3.

puzzles.prompt: A 3 by 3 board has a corner square removed. Can the remaining 8 squares be covered by 4 dominoes?
puzzles.showed: A corner is of the majority colour, so 4 and 4 remain, and a covering exists.

puzzles.prompt: The numbers 12 and 18 are on a board. You may write the positive difference of any two numbers on the board, if it is not there already. When nothing more can be written, how many numbers are on the board?
puzzles.verify:
def close(nums):
    s = set(nums)
    while True:
        new = {abs(a - b) for a in s for b in s if a != b} - s
        if not new: return s
        s |= new
result = len(close((12, 18)))
puzzles.showed: Every number written is a multiple of gcd(12, 18) = 6 and at most 18: so 6, 12, 18.

puzzles.prompt: The same with 5 and 8 on the board at the start. How many numbers are on the board at the end?
puzzles.verify:
def close(nums):
    s = set(nums)
    while True:
        new = {abs(a - b) for a in s for b in s if a != b} - s
        if not new: return s
        s |= new
result = len(close((5, 8)))
puzzles.showed: The differences eventually produce gcd(5, 8) = 1, and then every number from 1 to 8.

puzzles.prompt: Five lamps in a circle are off. A move switches two neighbouring lamps. Can all five be on at once?
puzzles.showed: The number of lit lamps changes by -2, 0 or +2 and so stays even; five is odd.

puzzles.prompt: Six lamps in a circle are off, same move. What is the smallest number of moves that lights all six?
puzzles.showed: Three disjoint neighbouring pairs. Fewer moves switch at most four lamps.

puzzles.prompt: Three cups stand in a row. A move swaps two of them. After exactly five moves, can the cups be back in their original order?
puzzles.showed: Every swap changes the arrangement between "even" and "odd" (the parity of the number of out-of-order pairs). Five swaps leave an odd arrangement; the original order is even.

puzzles.prompt: And after exactly four moves?
puzzles.showed: Swap the same two cups four times.

puzzles.prompt: A board shows seven 1s and three 0s. You repeatedly erase two numbers and write 0 if they were equal and 1 if they were different. What is the last number?
puzzles.verify:
import itertools
def ends(s):
    if len(s) == 1: return {s[0]}
    out = set()
    for i, j in itertools.combinations(range(len(s)), 2):
        rest = tuple(sorted(s[:i] + s[i + 1:j] + s[j + 1:] + (int(s[i] != s[j]),)))
        out |= ends(rest)
    return out
import functools
ends = functools.lru_cache(None)(ends)
e = ends((1,) * 7 + (0,) * 3)
result = next(iter(e)) if len(e) == 1 else None
puzzles.showed: Each move keeps the parity of the number of 1s (two 1s vanish, or nothing changes). Seven is odd, so a single 1 remains.

puzzles.prompt: Twenty lockers are closed. For each k from 1 to 20 in turn, every locker whose number is a multiple of k has its door switched (open to closed or closed to open). How many lockers are open at the end?
puzzles.verify:
state = [0] * 21
for k in range(1, 21):
    for m in range(k, 21, k): state[m] ^= 1
result = sum(state)
puzzles.showed: Locker n is switched once for each divisor of n. Divisors come in pairs d and n/d, except when n is a perfect square: so only 1, 4, 9 and 16 end open.

puzzles.prompt: At a gathering of five people, some pairs shake hands. The number of people who shook hands an odd number of times is:
puzzles.verify:
import itertools
edges = list(itertools.combinations(range(5), 2))
par = set()
for mask in range(1 << 10):
    deg = [0] * 5
    for i, (a, b) in enumerate(edges):
        if mask >> i & 1: deg[a] += 1; deg[b] += 1
    par.add(sum(d % 2 for d in deg) % 2)
result = 0 if par == {0} else 1 if par == {1} else 2
puzzles.showed: Adding up everyone's handshakes counts each handshake twice, so the total is even. A sum is even only if it has an even number of odd terms.

puzzles.prompt: A pile of 10 stones. A move removes exactly 1 or exactly 4 stones; whoever takes the last stone wins. Who wins?
puzzles.showed: Label small piles: the losing ones for the mover are 0, 2, 5, 7, 10, ... (remainder 0 or 2 mod 5). From those every move leaves remainder 1, 3 or 4, and from those you can always return to 0 or 2.

puzzles.prompt: Same game (remove 1 or 4) with 13 stones. How many should the first player take?
puzzles.showed: Leave 12, which has remainder 2 mod 5. Taking 4 would leave 9, a winning pile for the opponent.

puzzles.prompt: Two piles of 3 and 5 stones. A move removes any positive number from one pile, or the same positive number from both. Whoever takes the last stone wins. Who wins?
puzzles.showed: Labelling small positions gives the losing pairs (1, 2), (3, 5), (4, 7), ... Every move from (3, 5) can be answered by moving to (1, 2) or by finishing.

puzzles.prompt: Same rules with piles of 4 and 6. Who wins?
puzzles.showed: Take one stone from each pile, handing over the losing pair (3, 5).

puzzles.prompt: Three piles of 2 stones each; a move removes any positive number from one pile; last stone wins. How many different winning first moves are there (counting the choice of pile)?
puzzles.showed: Remove one whole pile, leaving two equal piles to copy on. Any of the three piles will do; taking a single stone leaves 1, 2, 2 with XOR 1.

puzzles.prompt: Four piles of 1 stone each, same rules. Who wins?
puzzles.showed: Four moves are made whatever happens, and the second player makes the fourth. (Equivalently: 1 xor 1 xor 1 xor 1 = 0.)

puzzles.prompt: The number 9 is on a board. A move subtracts 1, or halves the number if it is even. The player who makes the number 0 wins. Who wins?
puzzles.showed: From an odd number of at least 5 the only move is to an even number of at least 4. From there the opponent subtracts 1 back to an odd number of at least 5, or from 4 halves to 2, which also loses for the player to move.

puzzles.prompt: The number 1 is on a board. A move multiplies it by 2 or by 3. The player who first makes the number 30 or more wins. Who wins?
puzzles.showed: Work backwards. From 10 to 29 the mover wins at once. From 5 to 9 both moves land in 10 to 29, so those lose. From 2, 3 and 4 the mover can reach 6 or 8, so those win. From 1 both moves (2 and 3) hand over a winning number.

puzzles.prompt: A chocolate bar of 2 rows and 3 columns; the top-left square is poisoned. A move chooses a remaining square and eats it together with every remaining square below it or to its right (or both). Whoever eats the poisoned square loses. Who wins?
puzzles.showed: The first player eats only the bottom-right square. In fact the first player wins on any rectangle: if eating just the far corner were a losing move, the opponent's winning reply could have been played as a first move instead.

puzzles.prompt: A strip of 4 cells in a row. A move colours a cell that is not next to an already coloured cell. The player who cannot move loses. Who wins?
puzzles.showed: Whichever cell is coloured first, exactly one more cell can be coloured afterwards. Two moves, so the second player makes the last one.

puzzles.prompt: The same game on a strip of 5 cells. Who wins?
puzzles.showed: Colour the middle cell. Only the two end cells remain, one move each: three moves in all.

puzzles.prompt: The numbers 8 and 5 are on a board. A move subtracts a positive multiple of the smaller number from the larger, keeping it non-negative. The player who makes one of the numbers 0 wins. Who wins?
puzzles.showed: Every move is forced: (8, 5), (5, 3), (3, 2), (2, 1). It is then the second player's turn, who subtracts 2 x 1 from the 2 and reaches 0.

puzzles.prompt: Same game with 10 and 4. Who wins?
puzzles.showed: The first player has a choice (subtract 4 or 8), and a player with a choice can decide who gets the next forced position: subtract 4, leaving (6, 4); the opponent must go to (4, 2), and then 4 - 2 x 2 = 0.

puzzles.prompt: A pile of 20 stones. A move removes at least one stone and at most half of the pile. The player who cannot move (a single stone is left) loses. How many stones should the first player take?
puzzles.showed: The losing piles are 1, 3, 7, 15, 31, ...: one less than a power of two. From 15 every move leaves between 8 and 14, and from any of those the opponent can go to 7. So leave 15.

puzzles.prompt: How many numbers from 0 to 31 have exactly two binary digits equal to 1?
puzzles.verify: result = sum(1 for x in range(32) if bin(x).count('1') == 2)
puzzles.showed: Choose which two of the five places hold the 1s: 10 ways.

puzzles.prompt: What is the AND of all the numbers 12, 13, 14, 15?
puzzles.showed: They share the leading digits 11 and differ in everything below: 1100.

puzzles.prompt: What is the OR of all the numbers from 5 to 9?
puzzles.verify:
import functools, operator
result = functools.reduce(operator.or_, range(5, 10))
puzzles.showed: 7 supplies the three low bits and 8 supplies the next one: 1111.

puzzles.prompt: What is 6 XOR 15?
puzzles.verify: result = 6 ^ 15
puzzles.showed: XOR with 1111 flips all four low bits: 0110 becomes 1001. It is the same as 15 - 6.

puzzles.prompt: What is 44 AND 43?
puzzles.verify: result = 44 & 43
puzzles.showed: Subtracting 1 turns the lowest 1 into 0 and the zeros below it into 1s; the AND then removes exactly that lowest 1. 44 is 101100, the result 101000.

puzzles.prompt: How many binary digits of 1023 are 1?
puzzles.verify: result = bin(1023).count('1')
puzzles.showed: 1023 is one less than 1024, so it is ten 1s in a row.

puzzles.prompt: How many pairs a < b of numbers from 1 to 8 have a XOR b = 3?
puzzles.verify: result = sum(1 for a in range(1, 9) for b in range(a + 1, 9) if a ^ b == 3)
puzzles.showed: b must be a XOR 3, so each number has exactly one partner: (1, 2), (4, 7), (5, 6). The partner of 3 is 0 and of 8 is 11, both out of range.

puzzles.prompt: What is the largest value of a AND b for two different numbers a, b from 1 to 10?
puzzles.verify: result = max(a & b for a in range(1, 11) for b in range(1, 11) if a != b)
puzzles.showed: 8 AND 9 = 8. To beat 8 both numbers would need the 8s bit and a common lower bit, but 8, 9 and 10 share no lower bit.

puzzles.prompt: Among the numbers 4, 9, 10, 15, what is the smallest XOR of two different ones?
puzzles.verify:
import itertools
result = min(a ^ b for a, b in itertools.combinations((4, 9, 10, 15), 2))
puzzles.showed: 9 XOR 10 = 3. The smallest XOR in a set is always between two numbers that are neighbours in sorted order.

puzzles.prompt: How many ordered pairs (a, b) of non-negative whole numbers have a + b = 15 and a XOR b = 15?
puzzles.verify: result = sum(1 for a in range(16) if a ^ (15 - a) == 15)
puzzles.showed: Sum equals XOR means the AND is 0: no place is shared. Each of the four bits of 15 goes to a or to b: 16 ways.

puzzles.prompt: What is the largest power of two that is at most 100?
puzzles.verify: result = 1 << (100).bit_length() - 1
puzzles.showed: 64; the next one, 128, is too large. It is the value of the highest 1 in the binary form of 100.

puzzles.prompt: For how many x from 0 to 15 is x XOR 5 larger than x?
puzzles.verify: result = sum(1 for x in range(16) if x ^ 5 > x)
puzzles.showed: XOR with 5 flips the 4s bit and the 1s bit. The result is larger exactly when the higher of the flipped bits, the 4s bit, was 0: half of the sixteen numbers.

puzzles.prompt: Ten coins show heads. A move turns over exactly four coins. What is the smallest number of moves that makes all ten show tails?
puzzles.showed: Two moves flip at most 8 coins, so at least 3 are needed. Three moves make 12 flips: every coin once and one coin three times. Parity does not forbid it because each move changes the number of heads by an even amount and 10 is even.

puzzles.prompt: For how many n from 1 to 30 can plus and minus signs be put in front of 1, 2, ..., n so that the total is 0?
puzzles.showed: The total with all pluses must be even, so n is 0 or 3 mod 4; and for every such n a split into two equal halves exists (extend a solution for n to n + 4). That is 3, 4, 7, 8, ..., 27, 28: fourteen values.

puzzles.prompt: Eight lamps in a circle, all off. A move switches two neighbouring lamps. How many different on/off patterns can be reached, counting the starting one?
puzzles.showed: The only invariant is that the number of lit lamps is even, and every pattern with an even number of lit lamps is reachable (two lit lamps anywhere can be made by a chain of neighbouring switches). Half of the 256 patterns.

puzzles.prompt: A knight starts on a corner of a chessboard. On how many different squares can it be after exactly four moves?
puzzles.showed: Only squares of the corner's own colour are possible after an even number of moves (32 of them), and those too far away drop out. There is no shortcut for the exact count: it is a four-step expansion of a set.

puzzles.prompt: Chameleons again: 21 in all, in three colours; when two of different colours meet both turn into the third. For how many ordered triples (red, green, blue) adding up to 21 can they all end up one colour?
puzzles.showed: Two of the counts must be equal mod 3, because their difference changes only by multiples of 3 and has to reach 0. Since the total is a multiple of 3, two equal residues force all three to be equal: the count is the number of triples with all residues equal, 85 of the 253.

puzzles.prompt: The numbers 1 to 7 are on a board. A move erases two numbers and writes their difference (larger minus smaller). How many different numbers can be the last one left?
puzzles.showed: The last number has the parity of the total, 28, so it is even; it is at most 7, so at most 6. All of 0, 2, 4, 6 can be reached.

puzzles.prompt: How many triples of pile sizes 1 <= a <= b <= c <= 10 are losing for the player to move in the game "remove any number from one pile, last stone wins"?
puzzles.verify: result = sum(1 for a in range(1, 11) for b in range(a, 11) for c in range(b, 11) if a ^ b ^ c == 0)
puzzles.showed: The position loses exactly when a XOR b XOR c = 0, so c is forced by a and b; count the pairs for which a XOR b lands in range and in order.

puzzles.prompt: A move removes 2, 5 or 7 stones from a pile; a player who cannot move loses. For how many pile sizes from 0 to 100 does the player to move lose?
puzzles.showed: Label piles from 0 upward until the labels repeat. Here the period is 22 and the losing remainders are 0, 1, 4, 10, 13, 14: four full periods up to 87, then 88, 89, 92 and 98.

puzzles.prompt: How many ordered pairs (a, b) with 0 <= a, b < 64 have a AND b = 0?
puzzles.verify: result = sum(1 for a in range(64) for b in range(64) if a & b == 0)
puzzles.showed: In each of the six binary places the bits are (0,0), (0,1) or (1,0): 3^6.

puzzles.prompt: Add up a AND b over all pairs a < b of numbers from 1 to 50.
puzzles.verify: result = sum(a & b for a in range(1, 51) for b in range(a + 1, 51))
puzzles.showed: For each binary place count the numbers c having that bit; the place contributes its value times c(c-1)/2.

puzzles.prompt: The row 1 2 3 4 5 6. A move takes three neighbouring entries a b c and reverses them to c b a. How many different rows can be reached, counting the starting one?
puzzles.showed: Reversing three neighbours swaps two entries two places apart and leaves the middle one alone, so every number stays on positions of the same parity. Within the odd positions and within the even positions every arrangement is reachable: 3! x 3!.

puzzles.prompt: In how many ways can a 4 by 4 board be covered by dominoes?
puzzles.showed: Fill the board square by square, always covering the first empty square in one of two ways, and count the completions; the state is the set of covered squares, or just the profile of the current column.

puzzles.prompt: Twelve lamps in a row, all off. A move switches four neighbouring lamps. How many different patterns can be reached, counting the starting one?
puzzles.showed: There are nine moves, their order does not matter and repeating one cancels it, so a pattern is a subset of moves. Different subsets give different patterns (look at the leftmost move in which they differ), so the count is 2 to the power 9.

puzzles.prompt: Nine lamps in a circle, all off. A move switches three neighbouring lamps. How many different patterns can be reached, counting the starting one?
puzzles.showed: Nine moves, but they are not independent: the three moves starting at positions 0, 3, 6 together switch every lamp once, and so do those starting at 1, 4, 7 and at 2, 5, 8. Those two coincidences halve the count twice: 2 to the power 7.

puzzles.prompt: Sixteen lamps in a 4 by 4 grid, all off. A move switches every lamp in one row or one column. How many different patterns can be reached, counting the starting one?
puzzles.showed: Eight moves; using all four rows and all four columns changes nothing, and that is the only coincidence. So 2 to the power 7.

puzzles.prompt: The row 1 2 3 4 5. A move swaps any two entries. How many different rows can be reached in exactly four moves?
puzzles.showed: Four swaps always give an even arrangement, so at most half of the 120. And every even arrangement needs 0, 2 or 4 swaps, which can be padded to exactly four by swapping the same pair twice.

puzzles.prompt: Start from the pair (1, 1). A move replaces (a, b) by (a + b, b) or by (a, a + b). How many pairs with both numbers at most 20 can be reached?
puzzles.showed: The gcd never changes, so only pairs with gcd 1 are possible; and every such pair is reached, by running the subtraction process backwards from it to (1, 1). So this counts the ordered pairs up to 20 with no common factor.

puzzles.prompt: A move removes 1, 2, 4, 8, ... (any power of two) stones from a pile; a player who cannot move loses. For how many pile sizes from 1 to 100 does the player to move lose?
puzzles.showed: No power of two is a multiple of 3, so from a multiple of 3 every move leaves a non-multiple; and from a non-multiple you can remove 1 or 2 to reach a multiple. The losing piles are the multiples of 3.

puzzles.prompt: A move removes a perfect square number of stones (1, 4, 9, ...) from a pile; a player who cannot move loses. For how many pile sizes from 1 to 100 does the player to move lose?
puzzles.showed: There is no formula here. Label the piles one by one from 0: a pile loses if every square you can remove leads to a winning pile. The losing piles begin 2, 5, 7, 10, 12, 15, 17, 20, 22, 34, ...

puzzles.prompt: How many ordered triples (a, b, c) of numbers from 0 to 7 have a XOR b XOR c = 0?
puzzles.verify: result = sum(1 for a in range(8) for b in range(8) for c in range(8) if a ^ b ^ c == 0)
puzzles.showed: Choose a and b freely; c is then forced to be a XOR b, which is again between 0 and 7.

puzzles.prompt: For how many n from 1 to 1000 is 1 XOR 2 XOR ... XOR n equal to 0?
puzzles.verify:
import itertools, operator
result = sum(1 for v in itertools.accumulate(range(1, 1001), operator.xor) if v == 0)
puzzles.showed: The running XOR is n, 1, n + 1, 0 as n mod 4 is 0, 1, 2, 3. So it is 0 exactly when n is 3 mod 4.

puzzles.prompt: Write the numbers 1 to 1000 in binary. How many digits 1 are written in total?
puzzles.verify: result = sum(bin(i).count('1') for i in range(1, 1001))
puzzles.showed: Count place by place. In the place worth 2^k the digits run in blocks of 2^k zeros then 2^k ones; count the complete blocks up to 1000 and the leftover part, and add over the ten places.

puzzles.prompt: How many pairs a < b of numbers from 0 to 31 differ in exactly one binary digit?
puzzles.verify: result = sum(1 for a in range(32) for b in range(a + 1, 32) if bin(a ^ b).count('1') == 1)
puzzles.showed: Each of the 32 numbers has 5 neighbours (flip one of its five digits), and each pair is counted from both ends: 32 x 5 / 2.

puzzles.prompt: Nine chips sit on the point 0 of a number line. A move picks a point with at least two chips and sends one chip one step left and one chip one step right. How many moves are made before the process stops?
puzzles.verify:
c, moves = {0: 9}, 0
while True:
    p = next((k for k, v in c.items() if v >= 2), None)
    if p is None: break
    c[p] -= 2; c[p - 1] = c.get(p - 1, 0) + 1; c[p + 1] = c.get(p + 1, 0) + 1; moves += 1
result = moves
puzzles.showed: The sum of the squares of the chip positions grows by exactly 2 with every move. The final position is one chip on each of -4, ..., 4, with sum of squares 60, so 30 moves.

puzzles.prompt: How many orders of the numbers 1 to 5 have exactly four pairs that are out of order?
puzzles.verify:
import itertools
result = sum(1 for p in itertools.permutations(range(5)) if sum(1 for i in range(5) for j in range(i + 1, 5) if p[i] > p[j]) == 4)
puzzles.showed: Build the table by size: inserting the largest number into an order of k - 1 numbers adds between 0 and k - 1 out-of-order pairs. Row by row: 1; 1 1; 1 2 2 1; 1 3 5 6 5 3 1; and for five numbers the entry for four pairs.

puzzles.prompt: The string 1101001 is sorted (all 0s first) by swapping neighbouring characters. What is the smallest number of swaps?
puzzles.showed: Count the pairs (a 1, a later 0). Each swap of neighbours changes that count by exactly one, and the sorted string has none.

puzzles.prompt: How many binary strings of length 12 have no two 1s next to each other?
puzzles.verify:
import itertools, functools
strs = lambda n, alpha='01': (''.join(t) for t in itertools.product(alpha, repeat=n))
result = sum(1 for s in strs(12) if '11' not in s)
puzzles.showed: A valid string ends in 0 (any valid string of length n-1 before it) or in 01 (any valid string of length n-2 before it): the counts 2, 3, 5, 8, ... add the last two.

puzzles.prompt: How many binary strings of length 10 have five 0s and five 1s and, in every prefix, at least as many 1s as 0s?
puzzles.verify:
import itertools, functools
strs = lambda n, alpha='01': (''.join(t) for t in itertools.product(alpha, repeat=n))
result = sum(1 for s in strs(10) if s.count('1') == 5 and all(s[:k].count('1') >= s[:k].count('0') for k in range(1, 11)))
puzzles.showed: Read 1 as an opening bracket and 0 as a closing one: these are the correct bracket sequences of 5 pairs, C(10,5) / 6.

puzzles.prompt: How many substrings of 110100110 contain equally many 0s and 1s?
puzzles.verify:
s = '110100110'
result = sum(1 for i in range(9) for j in range(i + 1, 10) if s[i:j].count('0') * 2 == j - i)
puzzles.showed: Score +1 for a 1 and -1 for a 0 and take running totals from 0. A substring is balanced exactly when the totals at its two ends are equal: count equal pairs.

puzzles.prompt: An operation chooses a substring and inverts every character in it. What is the smallest number of operations that turns 0110100 into all 0s?
puzzles.showed: Pad with a 0 on each side and look at the boundaries between different neighbours. An operation changes at most two boundaries, and each block of 1s owns two: one operation per block of 1s.

puzzles.prompt: An operation deletes two neighbouring characters that are different (01 or 10). Starting from 1101110100, what is the shortest length you can reach?
puzzles.showed: Each deletion removes one 0 and one 1, so (number of 1s minus number of 0s) never changes; and while both kinds are present, some 0 sits next to some 1. The answer is the difference of the two counts.

puzzles.prompt: An operation deletes two neighbouring characters that are equal (00 or 11). Starting from 0110100110, what is the shortest length you can reach?
puzzles.showed: Process the characters with a stack: push a character unless it equals the top, in which case pop. The order of deletions does not matter, so the stack size at the end is the answer. (Equivalently: flip every second character and it becomes the 01/10 game.)

puzzles.prompt: How many binary strings of length 10 can be sorted with at most 3 swaps of neighbouring characters?
puzzles.verify:
import itertools, functools
strs = lambda n, alpha='01': (''.join(t) for t in itertools.product(alpha, repeat=n))
result = sum(1 for s in strs(10) if sum(1 for i in range(10) for j in range(i + 1, 10) if s[i] == '1' and s[j] == '0') <= 3)
puzzles.showed: The number of swaps needed is the number of pairs (1, later 0). Count strings by that number: a table over (length, pairs so far, number of 1s so far), or think of each 0 contributing the number of 1s before it.

puzzles.prompt: An operation swaps two characters that are exactly two positions apart. How many different strings can be reached from 1100110000, counting itself?
puzzles.showed: A character never changes the parity of its position, and within the odd positions (and within the even ones) any rearrangement is possible. With two 1s among the five odd positions and two among the five even ones: C(5,2) x C(5,2).

puzzles.prompt: How many binary strings of length 14 consist of exactly 4 blocks of equal characters?
puzzles.verify:
import itertools, functools
strs = lambda n, alpha='01': (''.join(t) for t in itertools.product(alpha, repeat=n))
result = sum(1 for s in strs(14) if sum(1 for i in range(13) if s[i] != s[i + 1]) == 3)
puzzles.showed: Choose the 3 places (out of 13 gaps) where the character changes, and the first character: 2 x C(13, 3).

puzzles.prompt: How many different non-empty strings can be obtained from 1101001 by deleting some characters (possibly none)?
puzzles.verify:
import itertools, functools
strs = lambda n, alpha='01': (''.join(t) for t in itertools.product(alpha, repeat=n))
s = '1101001'
result = len({''.join(s[i] for i in range(7) if m >> i & 1) for m in range(1, 128)})
puzzles.showed: Go left to right keeping D, the number of distinct subsequences so far including the empty one. A new character doubles D, minus the value D had just before the previous occurrence of the same character. Subtract 1 at the end for the empty one.

puzzles.prompt: How many binary strings of length 12 have an even number of places where two neighbouring characters differ?
puzzles.verify:
import itertools, functools
strs = lambda n, alpha='01': (''.join(t) for t in itertools.product(alpha, repeat=n))
result = sum(1 for s in strs(12) if sum(1 for i in range(11) if s[i] != s[i + 1]) % 2 == 0)
puzzles.showed: Walking along the string, each change flips the current character, so the number of changes is even exactly when the first and last characters are equal: half of all strings.

puzzles.prompt: What is the length of the longest substring of 1101101110110111 containing at most two 0s?
puzzles.verify:
s = '1101101110110111'
result = max(j - i for i in range(len(s)) for j in range(i + 1, len(s) + 1) if s[i:j].count('0') <= 2)
puzzles.showed: "At most two 0s" survives shrinking, so sweep with two ends: extend the right end, and move the left end while there are three 0s inside.

puzzles.prompt: For every binary string of length 6 count the pairs (a 1, a later 0). What is the sum of these counts over all 64 strings?
puzzles.verify:
import itertools, functools
strs = lambda n, alpha='01': (''.join(t) for t in itertools.product(alpha, repeat=n))
result = sum(1 for s in strs(6) for i in range(6) for j in range(i + 1, 6) if s[i] == '1' and s[j] == '0')
puzzles.showed: Fix a pair of positions i < j: it is a (1, 0) pair in exactly a quarter of the strings. There are 15 pairs of positions: 15 x 16.

puzzles.prompt: How many binary strings of length 10 contain 101 as a substring?
puzzles.verify:
import itertools, functools
strs = lambda n, alpha='01': (''.join(t) for t in itertools.product(alpha, repeat=n))
result = sum(1 for s in strs(10) if '101' in s)
puzzles.showed: Count the strings that avoid 101 with a small table (remember how much of the pattern the current ending matches: nothing, "1", or "10") and subtract from 1024.

puzzles.prompt: How many binary strings of length 16 have smallest period exactly 4 (the string is some block of length 4 repeated, and no shorter block works)?
puzzles.verify:
import itertools, functools
strs = lambda n, alpha='01': (''.join(t) for t in itertools.product(alpha, repeat=n))
per = lambda s: next(p for p in range(1, len(s) + 1) if all(s[i] == s[i - p] for i in range(p, len(s))))
result = sum(1 for s in strs(16) if per(s) == 4)
puzzles.showed: Sixteen strings are a block of length 4 repeated; remove those whose block itself has a shorter period (period 1 or 2): 16 - 4.

puzzles.prompt: What is the smallest number of characters to change in 0010110100 so that no two neighbouring characters are equal?
puzzles.verify:
import itertools, functools
strs = lambda n, alpha='01': (''.join(t) for t in itertools.product(alpha, repeat=n))
s = '0010110100'
result = min(sum(1 for a, b in zip(s, t) if a != b) for t in ('0101010101', '1010101010'))
puzzles.showed: There are only two alternating strings of each length. Count mismatches against one of them; the other needs (length minus that).

puzzles.prompt: How many substrings of abacabad are palindromes (counted by position, single letters included)?
puzzles.verify:
pal = lambda s: s == s[::-1]
s = 'abacabad'
result = sum(1 for i in range(8) for j in range(i + 1, 9) if pal(s[i:j]))
puzzles.showed: Go centre by centre: 15 centres (8 on letters, 7 between), and from each expand while the two sides match. Add up how far each one extends.

puzzles.prompt: How many palindromes of length 7 are there over an alphabet of 3 letters?
puzzles.verify:
import itertools, functools
strs = lambda n, alpha='01': (''.join(t) for t in itertools.product(alpha, repeat=n))
pal = lambda s: s == s[::-1]
result = sum(1 for s in strs(7, 'abc') if pal(s))
puzzles.showed: The first four letters are free and the rest are forced: 3^4.

puzzles.prompt: For how many n from 1 to 1000 is the binary form of n (without leading zeros) a palindrome?
puzzles.verify:
pal = lambda s: s == s[::-1]
result = sum(1 for n in range(1, 1001) if pal(bin(n)[2:]))
puzzles.showed: Count by length: a binary palindrome of length L starts and ends with 1 and its first half is otherwise free, 2^(ceil(L/2) - 1) of them. Do lengths 1 to 9 fully and handle length 10 (up to 1000) by hand.

puzzles.prompt: What is the smallest number of characters that must be inserted into abcbda to make it a palindrome?
puzzles.showed: It equals the length minus the longest palindromic subsequence (here abcba, of length 5): the letters outside that subsequence each need a partner inserted.

puzzles.prompt: What is the length of the longest palindrome that can be obtained from the word "character" by deleting letters?
puzzles.verify:
import itertools
s = 'character'
result = max(k for k in range(1, 10) for c in itertools.combinations(s, k) if c == c[::-1])
puzzles.showed: The longest palindromic subsequence is the longest common subsequence of the word and its reverse; here "carac".

puzzles.prompt: How many substrings of aabbccabc can have their letters rearranged into a palindrome?
puzzles.verify:
import collections
s = 'aabbccabc'
result = sum(1 for i in range(9) for j in range(i + 1, 10) if sum(v % 2 for v in collections.Counter(s[i:j]).values()) <= 1)
puzzles.showed: Keep a 3-bit mask of letter parities for each prefix. A substring works when its two prefix masks are equal or differ in exactly one bit: for each prefix, look up how many earlier prefixes have one of those four masks.

puzzles.prompt: How many strings of length 8 over the letters a, b, c contain no palindromic substring of length 2 or more?
puzzles.verify:
import itertools, functools
strs = lambda n, alpha='01': (''.join(t) for t in itertools.product(alpha, repeat=n))
pal = lambda s: s == s[::-1]
result = sum(1 for s in strs(8, 'abc') if not any(pal(s[i:j]) for i in range(8) for j in range(i + 2, 9)))
puzzles.showed: Any longer palindrome contains one of length 2 or 3 at its centre, so it is enough to forbid s_i = s_(i+1) and s_i = s_(i+2). Then the first two letters are any two different ones and every later letter is forced: 3 x 2.

puzzles.prompt: How many different palindromes occur as substrings of abracadabra?
puzzles.verify:
pal = lambda s: s == s[::-1]
s = 'abracadabra'
result = len({s[i:j] for i in range(11) for j in range(i + 1, 12) if pal(s[i:j])})
puzzles.showed: A string of length n has at most n different palindromic substrings, because appending a character creates at most one new one (the longest palindromic suffix). Here there are far fewer than 11.

puzzles.prompt: What is the smallest number of pieces into which abacdcabb can be cut so that every piece is a palindrome?
puzzles.showed: Let best(i) be the fewest pieces for the suffix starting at i: try every palindrome starting at i. Precompute which substrings are palindromes so each try is O(1).

puzzles.prompt: Seven words: ab, ba, abc, cba, a, aa, b. For how many ordered pairs of two different words is the first followed by the second a palindrome?
puzzles.verify:
pal = lambda s: s == s[::-1]
w = ['ab', 'ba', 'abc', 'cba', 'a', 'aa', 'b']
result = sum(1 for i in range(7) for j in range(7) if i != j and pal(w[i] + w[j]))
puzzles.showed: For each word and each way of splitting it into a prefix and a suffix: if the suffix is a palindrome, the reverse of the prefix can go after it; if the prefix is a palindrome, the reverse of the suffix can go before it. Look the needed word up in a set.

puzzles.prompt: How many binary strings of length 8 are a palindrome already, or become one after deleting exactly one character?
puzzles.verify:
import itertools, functools
strs = lambda n, alpha='01': (''.join(t) for t in itertools.product(alpha, repeat=n))
pal = lambda s: s == s[::-1]
result = sum(1 for s in strs(8) if pal(s) or any(pal(s[:i] + s[i + 1:]) for i in range(8)))
puzzles.showed: To test one string, walk in from both ends; at the first mismatch the deleted character must be one of those two, so try both and check that the rest is a palindrome.

puzzles.prompt: What is the smallest palindromic number greater than 123456?
puzzles.verify:
pal = lambda s: s == s[::-1]
result = next(n for n in range(123457, 200000) if pal(str(n)))
puzzles.showed: Mirror the left half: 123321 is too small, so add 1 to the left half (124) and mirror again.

puzzles.prompt: What is the smallest number of letters to change in abcdefba to make it a palindrome?
puzzles.verify:
s = 'abcdefba'
result = sum(1 for i in range(4) if s[i] != s[7 - i])
puzzles.showed: Compare each position with its mirror: every mismatched pair costs exactly one change. Here (c, f) and (d, e).

puzzles.prompt: How many binary strings of length 12 can be written as a palindrome followed by another palindrome (both non-empty)?
puzzles.verify:
import itertools, functools
strs = lambda n, alpha='01': (''.join(t) for t in itertools.product(alpha, repeat=n))
pal = lambda s: s == s[::-1]
result = sum(1 for s in strs(12) if any(pal(s[:k]) and pal(s[k:]) for k in range(1, 12)))
puzzles.showed: There is no neat formula for the count. To test one string, precompute for every position whether the prefix ending there and the suffix starting there are palindromes, and look for a split where both hold.

puzzles.prompt: What is the length of the longest prefix of abacabaxyz that is a palindrome?
puzzles.verify:
pal = lambda s: s == s[::-1]
s = 'abacabaxyz'
result = max(k for k in range(1, 11) if pal(s[:k]))
puzzles.showed: Build s + # + reverse(s) and compute, for its last position, the longest prefix that is also a suffix: that length is the answer, in one linear pass.

puzzles.prompt: How many strings of length 9 over {a, b} are palindromes whose prefix of length 6 is also a palindrome?
puzzles.verify:
import itertools, functools
strs = lambda n, alpha='01': (''.join(t) for t in itertools.product(alpha, repeat=n))
pal = lambda s: s == s[::-1]
result = sum(1 for s in strs(9, 'ab') if pal(s) and pal(s[:6]))
puzzles.showed: If a palindrome of length n has a palindromic prefix of length m, then n - m is a period of it. Here the period is 3, so the string is a block of length 3 repeated, and the block must itself be a palindrome: 2 x 2.

puzzles.prompt: The statement says n is at most 20, and you must choose some of the n items subject to a complicated condition. What do the constraints suggest?
options: Go through all 2^n subsets (about a million), or a table indexed by subsets
It must be solvable in linear time, so look for a formula
puzzles.showed: n up to 20 (sometimes 22) is the setter telling you that subsets are affordable. n up to 15 or 16 allows subsets of subsets; n up to 40 suggests splitting into two halves of 20.

puzzles.prompt: A problem has up to 10^4 test cases and says "the sum of n over all test cases does not exceed 2 x 10^5". What should you make sure of?
options: That the work per test depends only on its own n, including clearing arrays: never reset an array of size 2 x 10^5 for every test
That each test runs in under a millisecond
That the answers are printed in one line
puzzles.showed: The sum bound means an O(n) or O(n log n) pass per test is fine in total, but anything that costs "maximum n" per test (clearing a big array, a sieve) is multiplied by 10^4 tests.

puzzles.prompt: n is up to 10^5, the values are up to 10^6, and the question is about divisors or multiples of the values. What is the standard move?
options: For every pair of elements compute their gcd
Factorise every element by trial division up to its square root for each query
Index by value: count how often each value occurs, then for every d loop over its multiples
puzzles.showed: Looping over all multiples of every d up to V costs V/1 + V/2 + ... which is about V log V. Small values are an invitation to work on the value axis instead of the index axis.

puzzles.prompt: n is at most 500 and the problem is about choosing the best way to combine neighbouring elements. Which complexity is the setter pointing at?
options: About n^3: a table over all pairs (l, r) with a split point inside
puzzles.showed: 500^3 is 1.25 x 10^8, which is fine. A cubic bound with "neighbouring elements merge" almost always means a table over intervals.

puzzles.prompt: The input is a single number n up to 10^18 and the answer is some count. What can the solution not do?
options: Anything that loops up to n, or even up to the square root of n in the worst cases; expect a formula, or work on the digits or bits of n
puzzles.showed: With 10^18 you get about 60 steps (the bits), or about 18 (the decimal digits), or a closed form. Square root is 10^9, usually too slow.

puzzles.prompt: The task says: "make the largest of the group sums as small as possible". What is the first thing to try?
options: Try all ways of forming groups
Guess the answer x and ask "can it be done with every group at most x?"; that yes/no question switches once, so halve on x
puzzles.showed: "Minimise the maximum" and "maximise the minimum" are the classic signals. The check for a fixed x is usually a simple greedy.

puzzles.prompt: The statement ends with "print the answer modulo 998244353". What does that tell you about the problem?
options: It is a counting problem (or an expected value written as a fraction): think combinatorics or a table of counts, and take the remainder at every step
puzzles.showed: A prime modulus means the true answer is astronomically large. For expected values it also means "divide" becomes "multiply by the modular inverse".

puzzles.prompt: You are given a start configuration, an allowed operation, and asked whether a target configuration can be reached. What do you look for first?
options: Something no operation can change (a parity, a sum, a remainder, a count on certain positions), and check whether start and target agree on it
A shortest sequence of operations by search
A way to sort both configurations
puzzles.showed: If start and target differ on an invariant, the answer is no at once. If they agree, the next question is whether that invariant is the only obstacle, which needs a construction.

puzzles.prompt: Edges are deleted from a graph one at a time, and after each deletion you must report the number of connected components. All deletions are known in advance. What is the move?
options: Recompute the components from scratch after each deletion
Process the deletions backwards as insertions, merging components, and reverse the answers
Keep the graph sorted by degree
puzzles.showed: Merging is easy and splitting is hard. Whenever everything is known in advance and "undo" is easier than "do", run time backwards.

puzzles.prompt: Count the pairs i < j for which some relation between a_i and a_j holds. n is 2 x 10^5. What is the usual shape of the solution?
options: Sort and take the middle element
Go through j from left to right, and for each j count the earlier i that match, using a map or a counting structure of what has been seen
puzzles.showed: Fix one end, and turn "how many partners" into a look-up. The relation usually rearranges into "a_i equals something computed from a_j".

puzzles.prompt: The answer is the sum of f(subarray) over all subarrays, and n is 2 x 10^5, so there are about 2 x 10^10 subarrays. What do you do?
options: Swap the order: for each element (or each pair, or each bit), count in how many subarrays it contributes, and add value times count
Use a table over all (l, r)
puzzles.showed: A sum over structures of a sum over their parts equals a sum over parts of the number of structures containing them. This is the first thing to try on any "sum over all".

puzzles.prompt: An operation adds 1 to every element of a chosen stretch of an array. Reasoning about the array directly is getting nowhere. What change of view usually helps?
options: Look at the differences between neighbours: the operation changes only two of them
puzzles.showed: Stretch operations become two point changes on the difference array; equally, questions about stretch sums become questions about pairs of prefix sums.

puzzles.prompt: A two-player game on a pile of n stones with unusual move rules, and n can be 10^9. You have no idea who wins. What do you do?
options: Write a brute force that labels positions as winning or losing for n up to 50 or so, print it, and look for the pattern
Guess that the first player wins when n is odd
Simulate the game for the given n
puzzles.showed: Small cases by machine, then a pattern (a period, a parity, a special family of numbers), then a proof or at least a check against the brute force.

puzzles.prompt: The task: "print any permutation of 1..n with property P, or say none exists". You do not see the structure. What is the most reliable start?
options: Prove that an answer always exists
Start with the identity and apply random swaps until it works
Find answers for n = 1 to 8 by hand or brute force, note which n are impossible, and look for a rule that grows one answer into the next
puzzles.showed: The impossible small cases suggest the necessary condition; the possible ones suggest the construction.

puzzles.prompt: An operation can reduce a certain count by at most 2, and the goal is to bring that count to 0 in as few operations as possible. What is the natural plan?
options: Search over all sequences of operations
The answer is at least half the count; now look for operations that always remove exactly 2, and for what can prevent that
Always pick the operation that touches the most elements
puzzles.showed: Lower bound first. Then either you can always meet it, or the cases where you cannot reveal a second quantity, and the answer becomes the larger of two bounds.

puzzles.prompt: You suspect that the answer to a minimisation problem is never more than 2. How do you use that?
options: Prove that 2 operations always suffice, then you only need to recognise when 0 works and when 1 works
Ignore it and write the general algorithm
puzzles.showed: Many problems rated around 1600 to 2000 are exactly this: a short argument caps the answer at a tiny constant, and the remaining work is a check for each smaller value.

puzzles.prompt: A process is applied k times with k up to 10^18, but its state is a small object (say one of at most 10^5 possibilities). What makes this tractable?
options: The states must repeat: find where the cycle starts and its length, then jump ahead using k modulo the cycle length
puzzles.showed: A deterministic process on finitely many states is eventually periodic. (When the step is a fixed map on positions, doubling also works: precompute where 1, 2, 4, 8, ... steps lead.)

puzzles.prompt: The answer does not depend on the order of the input elements, and you need to pair them up or choose a subset. What is almost always the first step?
options: Sort them, and then ask what the best choice is for the smallest or largest element
puzzles.showed: Sorting gives structure for free: the extreme element usually has an obviously best partner, and after sorting most choices become "a prefix", "a suffix" or "neighbours".

puzzles.prompt: You must count how many of n given lines (each as two points with integer coordinates) are parallel to each other. Comparing slopes as decimals is failing. What is the fix?
options: Give each direction a canonical form: divide (dx, dy) by their gcd and fix the sign, then compare the pairs exactly
puzzles.showed: Whenever "the same" is not literal equality (directions, fractions, rotations of a string, sets), normalise each object to one representative and compare those.

puzzles.prompt: A loop keeps replacing an element by half of itself until it reaches 0, and this may happen to every element after each of q queries. It looks like q x n work. Why is it actually fine?
options: Each element can be halved only about 30 times in total, so the total work over the whole run is about 30 n
puzzles.showed: Count the total over the whole run instead of per query: each element is pushed and popped once, each value halves or grows by a constant factor only log times, a pointer only moves forward.

puzzles.prompt: Your solution passes when you run each sample test alone, but gives wrong answers when several tests are in one input. What is the first thing to check?
options: State left over from the previous test: global arrays, counters, maps or flags that were not cleared, or input that was not fully read
puzzles.showed: It is the most common multi-test bug. A habit that prevents it: declare everything inside the per-test function, and always read the entire test before printing an early answer.

puzzles.prompt: n is 2 x 10^5 and the values are up to 10^9. You add up products of pairs of values. The samples pass but the judge says wrong answer. What is the likely cause?
options: Overflow: a product of two such values needs 64 bits, and a sum of many of them needs a modulus or even more care
puzzles.showed: Estimate the largest intermediate value before coding: 10^9 x 10^9 = 10^18 just fits in 64 bits signed, and one more addition may not.

puzzles.prompt: A correct O(n log n) solution with n = 10^6 gets "time limit exceeded" in C++. It reads with cin and prints each answer with endl. What should you change first?
options: Turn off stream synchronisation, untie cin, and print with a newline character instead of endl, which flushes every time
puzzles.showed: Flushing a million times and synchronised streams can cost more than the algorithm. Two lines at the top of main and "\n" fix it.

puzzles.prompt: There are n items and m statements of the form "items a and b must be in different groups", with two groups available. What is this, in standard terms?
options: A graph with the items as vertices and the statements as edges: the question is whether it can be two-coloured, that is, has no odd cycle
puzzles.showed: Pairwise constraints are edges. "Must differ" gives two-colouring; "must be equal" gives components; a mixture gives components with a parity.

puzzles.prompt: On a tree with 2 x 10^5 vertices you need the sum, over all pairs of vertices, of the distance between them. What is the standard move?
options: For each edge, count the pairs it separates (size of one side times size of the other) and add those up
Run a search from every vertex
puzzles.showed: Sums over all paths of a tree are computed edge by edge (or vertex by vertex) from subtree sizes.

puzzles.prompt: A grid where stepping onto some cells is free and onto others costs 1; you need the cheapest route. Which tool fits exactly?
options: A table filled row by row
A breadth-first search with a double-ended queue: free steps go to the front, costly steps to the back
puzzles.showed: With only costs 0 and 1 the priority queue of the general method can be replaced by a deque, giving linear time.

puzzles.prompt: For many pairs of vertices you are asked for a route whose largest edge is as small as possible. What structure answers all of them?
options: Add edges in increasing order with a union-find: two vertices become connected exactly when the threshold reaches their answer (equivalently, use the minimum spanning tree)
puzzles.showed: "Smallest possible largest edge" is about connectivity under a threshold, not about sums of lengths.

puzzles.prompt: Many queries ask for the XOR of a stretch of an array. What is the standard preparation?
options: Prefix XORs: the XOR of a stretch is the XOR of two prefix values, because equal parts cancel
A sorted copy of the array
puzzles.showed: Anything with an "undo" (addition, XOR, multiplication modulo a prime) works with prefixes; things without one (minimum, gcd) need a different structure.

puzzles.prompt: You must choose numbers to make some bitwise result (AND, OR or XOR) as large as possible. How should you think about it?
options: Decide the bits from the highest down: a higher bit is worth more than all lower bits together, so secure it if you can and then restrict to the choices that keep it
puzzles.showed: Greedy from the top bit is correct because 2^k exceeds the sum of all lower powers. Each bit becomes a yes/no feasibility question.

puzzles.prompt: Your solution gets a wrong answer on a hidden test and you cannot find the bug by reading the code. What is the most effective next step?
options: Write a slow, obviously correct brute force and a random generator for tiny inputs, and compare the two until they differ
puzzles.showed: A failing input with n = 5 usually shows the bug in a minute. It also catches wrong ideas, not only typing mistakes. The app has this built in on every problem page.
